title: European rights court bars Romanian lawyer for 2 years over AI citations
content:
Romanian lawyer barred for two years from representing applicants before the Court over unverified AI-generated citations
			
On 13 November 2026 the President of the Court decided to exclude a Romanian lawyer from representing or otherwise assisting litigants before the Court, for a period of two years.
This came after the Chamber that was dealing with the application in which the lawyer was acting as one of two representatives found that the observations which she had submitted on the case contained numerous errors concerning the Court’s case-law. These included the citation of non-existent (“hallucinated”) cases; the citation of fictitious paragraphs in genuine judgments and decisions of the Court; and the citation of existing case-law that was irrelevant to the propositions advanced or that plainly contradicted the submissions they were intended to support.
The lawyer acknowledged that she had used Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools to draft the observations and described the mistakes as “inaccuracies” and “citation errors”. The Chamber found that the lawyer’s submissions contained a pattern of numerous, repeated, substantive errors rather than isolated citation mistakes and concluded that her conduct fell short of the professional and ethical duties imposed by the Court, duties that are also found in domestic law.
The Chamber submitted a reasoned proposal to the President of the Court that the lawyer be excluded from representing applicants before the Court for two years. The President approved that proposal.

report.summary: The European Court of Human Rights barred a Romanian lawyer for two years after she submitted observations containing fabricated and misattributed AI-generated case citations.
report.background: Generative AI tools have spread rapidly through legal practice, promising faster drafting and research. But large language models frequently 'hallucinate' case law, inventing judgments, paragraphs, or quotations that sound authoritative but do not exist. Courts in the United States, United Kingdom, and elsewhere have already sanctioned lawyers for filing briefs with fake AI-generated citations. The European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) has now taken one of the strongest enforcement actions by an international tribunal. The case reflects growing concern that AI-assisted legal work can undermine the integrity of judicial proceedings if citations are not independently verified. It also highlights the tension between efficiency gains from AI and the professional duty of candour and accuracy that lawyers owe to courts.
key_points: The ECHR President excluded a Romanian lawyer from representing applicants for two years after a Chamber found her submitted observations contained numerous case-law errors, including citations to non-existent 'hallucinated' cases, fictitious paragraphs in real judgments, and irrelevant or contradictory authorities.

The lawyer acknowledged using AI tools to draft the observations and described the problems as 'inaccuracies' and 'citation errors.' The Chamber rejected that framing, finding a pattern of repeated, substantive mistakes rather than isolated citation slips.

The Chamber concluded her conduct fell short of the professional and ethical duties imposed by the Court, which are also reflected in domestic law. It submitted a reasoned proposal to the President, who approved the two-year exclusion.

The decision signals that international courts will treat unverified AI-generated citations as potential professional misconduct, not merely a technical glitch, and may impose direct consequences on lawyers' rights to practice before them.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the ruling adds pressure on legal AI vendors to build citation verification, retrieval grounding, and audit trails into their products. Developers should prioritise retrieval-augmented generation, source checking, uncertainty flags, and human-in-the-loop review rather than fluent but unverified output. For legal professionals and regular users, it is a warning that AI-generated legal research must be independently confirmed against primary sources. Courts may increasingly require disclosure of AI use or impose certification duties. The case could accelerate demand for trustworthy legal AI tools and for clear professional guidelines on generative AI, while raising liability questions for lawyers who rely on automated drafting without adequate checks.
report.tools: To follow up, watch the Free Law Project's CourtListener API for verifying real case law, and open-source hallucination-detection projects such as SelfCheckGPT and RAGAS for testing AI outputs. LangChain and LlamaIndex support retrieval-augmented generation with citations, while LegalBench offers benchmarks for legal reasoning. Commercial legal AI platforms such as Harvey and CoCounsel are also worth monitoring for citation-grounding features.
